s: Fire became known to mankind only after the first men had endured hardship. Knowledge of its usefulness helped them develop a more secure way of life.

s: Living creatures were said to arise from heat and moisture after the earth had begun to harden. Those with more heat became flying creatures, those with more earth became creeping things, and watery creatures moved into the water.

s: Early men first used confused words without fixed meanings. By degrees they spoke articulately, assigned terms to things, and developed different languages and dialects after spreading into various parts of the world.

l: human arts and inventions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK L
s: Human arts and inventions arose through necessity and experience. Men learned to use caves, preserve food, make use of fire, and develop other conveniences, aided by their hands, speech, and rational soul.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Diodorus first discusses the barbarians, especially the Egyptians, before turning to the history of the Grecians. The account then describes Osiris and Isis, their reign and civilizing works, the founding or disputed founding of Thebes, and the discoveries associated with agriculture, bread, wine, language, and the arts. Finally, Osiris begins a world expedition with Isis's advisers, Hercules, Apollo, Anubis, Pan, and others to teach cultivation and improve human life.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The Grecians are to be discussed after the barbarians, so that their history will not be confused with the antiquities of foreign peoples.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Egypt is presented as the country where the first humans were created and where the chief production of living things is said to have occurred. The account begins with Egypt because its gods, star observations, and famous deeds were especially celebrated.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The Nile is described as exceptionally fruitful and able to produce or support many animals and kinds of food, including canes, the lote-tree fruit, and the Egyptian bean.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Near Thebes, the Egyptians report that large mice are spontaneously formed, with some already animated in their front parts while the rest remain shaped like soil. Thebes is also said to have been built by Osiris, although its first founder is disputed.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The Egyptians report that Egypt produced the first humans and that living creatures can arise from the heated mud left by the Nile. They also identify natural powers with gods and preserve customs honoring Isis, Osiris, and other benefactors.

l: the formation of the world, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: In the Egyptians' account of the creation of the world, the first humans and other living creatures arose in Egypt because of its climate, heat, and fertile soil.

l: first humans in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The first humans are said to have been formed in Egypt because of the country's favorable climate and the productive nature of the Nile.

l: spontaneous generation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The text describes animals arising from fertile soil and Nile mud, especially after the river returns to its channel and the sun dries the ground. Some creatures are said to be fully formed while others remain partly attached to the soil.

l: Sol, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The Egyptians regard the sun as one of two eternal chief gods and call it Osiris. Its rays are said to reach every part of the land and sea, giving it the appearance of possessing many eyes.

l: Selene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The Egyptians regard the moon as the other eternal chief god and call it Isis. They associate her horns with the moon's crescent shape and say that an ox is sacrificed to her.

l: Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Osiris is identified with the sun and, by some Greek mythologists, with Dionysius or Bacchus. He is said to have ruled Egypt, taught agriculture and the cultivation of vines, prohibited cannibalism, built Thebes, and later led an expedition through the inhabited world.

l: Isis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Isis is identified with the moon and with Ceres. She is said to have discovered the preparation of bread from wheat and barley, established laws for human society, ruled Egypt during Osiris's expedition, and received harvest offerings in memory of her discoveries.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Jupiter is the Egyptian name for the spirit or quickening influence that gives life to living creatures and is therefore regarded as the common parent of all things. Jupiter is also listed among the terrestrial gods who once ruled Egypt and is called Ammon by some.

l: Vulcan, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Vulcan is the Egyptian name for fire and is revered as a god who contributes greatly to the generation and perfection of all beings. Some Egyptian priests say he was the first king because he discovered and preserved the use of fire.

l: earth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The earth is described as the common womb of all productions and is called Metera by the Egyptians. The Greeks later altered the name into Demetra.

l: water, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Water or moisture is called Oceanus by the ancients, a name interpreted as a nourishing mother. The Egyptians identify their Nile with Oceanus and say that the gods were born there.

l: air, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The air is associated with Minerva and is regarded as naturally incorruptible and situated in the highest part of the universe.

l: Minerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Minerva is the name given to the air and is called the daughter of Jupiter and a virgin. She is also called Tritogeneia because the air changes its natural qualities in spring, summer, and winter.

l: five elemental qualities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: The five qualities through which the sun and moon perfect all things are identified as a quickening spirit, heat or fire, dryness or earth, moisture or water, and air. The Egyptians treated these five as gods.

l: fire, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Fire is called Vulcan and is honored for its contribution to the generation and perfection of all beings. Its use is said to have been discovered when lightning set a tree in the mountains ablaze.

l: Hermes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Hermes is praised for extraordinary ingenuity and is said to have taught articulate speech, named many things, invented letters, established worship of the gods, observed the stars, invented music and arithmetic, and taught wrestling. He served as Osiris's sacred scribe and chief adviser.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Saturn is said to have ruled Egypt after Vulcan and to have married his sister Rhea. In another account, he is associated with the parentage of Osiris and Isis.

l: Juno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Juno is listed among the gods who are said to have ruled Egypt. In one account, she and Jupiter were the parents of five gods born on the five intercalary days.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Apollo is described as Osiris's brother and companion on his expedition. He is said to have discovered the laurel-tree, which was dedicated especially to him.

l: Osiris and Isis's reign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Osiris and Isis are said to have ruled Egypt and to have benefited humankind through agriculture, law, religious institutions, and the improvement of food. Osiris later entrusted the government of Egypt to Isis while he undertook his expedition.

l: bread, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Isis is credited with discovering how to make bread from wheat and barley. The change from uncultivated plants to bread helped restrain people from killing and eating one another.

l: wheat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Wheat formerly grew among common herbs and grass, but Isis discovered its use in bread-making. Wheat was carried in processions during festivals of Isis and offered as a first fruit.

l: barley, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Barley, like wheat, was used by Isis in the first making of bread. Egyptians carried barley in honor of Isis's discovery.

l: agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Osiris taught the methods of tillage and the proper management of the earth's fruits, while Isis introduced the use of wheat and barley for bread. Agriculture formed part of Osiris's larger effort to civilize humanity.

l: Thebes's founding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Thebes is reported to have been built by Osiris and named after his mother, later receiving the names Diospolis and Thebes. Egyptian historians and priests disagree, with some attributing its foundation to a later king.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Osiris is said to have been brought up in Nysa, a town of Arabia the Happy near Egypt. Near Nysa he supposedly discovered the use of the vine and began drinking and teaching others to use wine.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Osiris is credited with discovering the use of the vine, planting it near Nysa, and teaching people how to cultivate it, harvest grapes, and preserve wine.

l: Osiris's world expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: After settling affairs in Egypt, Osiris entrusted the kingdom to Isis and set out with an army through the inhabited world. He intended to teach people to plant vines and sow wheat and barley, civilize them, and gain lasting honor by benefiting humankind.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Hercules, described as Osiris's near kinsman, was left as general of all the forces within Osiris's dominions. He was admired for his courage and bodily strength.

l: Anubis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Anubis, one of Osiris's sons, accompanied him on his expedition and is described as a valiant man. He wore a coat of mail covered with a dog's skin, which is given as a reason Egyptians worshipped dogs.

l: Pan, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, We shall first speak of the barbarians; not that we judge them
s: Pan accompanied Osiris on his expedition and was highly revered by the Egyptians. They erected images and statues of him and built a city in Thebides called Chemmin, interpreted as Pan's city.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris travels through Ethiopia, Arabia, India, Asia, and Europe, teaching agriculture, founding cities, and establishing governors and tribute collectors. After returning, he is murdered and dismembered by his brother Typhon. Isis and her son Orus defeat Typhon, recover most of Osiris's body, and arrange his burial and worship. Egyptian priests preserve his memory through rites, animal worship, and claims about his tombs at Memphis and near Philas.

l: Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris vows to let his hair grow until he returns to Egypt and leads an expedition through Ethiopia, Arabia, India, Asia, and Europe. He teaches agriculture, founds cities, appoints rulers, promotes useful foods and drink, and is honored after death as a god.

l: Isis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris, helps avenge his death with Orus and takes possession of Egypt. She reassembles Osiris's body, assigns priests to bury and honor it, vows not to remarry, and is later worshipped as a goddess.

l: Typhon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Typhon, the wicked brother of Osiris, murders him and cuts his body into six-and-twenty pieces, distributing them among his confederates. Isis and Orus later avenge Osiris's death upon Typhon and his accomplices.

l: Orus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Orus, the son of Isis, assists her in avenging Osiris's death and defeating Typhon and his accomplices.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Egypt is ruled by Osiris and later by Isis after she defeats Typhon. Its priests maintain rites for Osiris, and its people venerate sacred animals associated with him.

l: Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris travels through Ethiopia, teaches its inhabitants husbandry and tillage, builds several cities, and leaves governors and tribute collectors there.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: The Nile overflows its banks during the dog-days and drowns much of Egypt, especially the region governed by Prometheus. Hercules repairs the breaches and confines the river to its channel, while the river is said to have borne several names, including Oceaines, Eagle, Egyptus, and Nileus.

l: Osiris's world expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris's expedition passes through Ethiopia, Arabia, India, Asia, and Europe. It includes musicians and satyrs, establishes cities and colonies, and spreads agriculture, useful foods, and drink.

l: Osiris's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris is murdered by his brother Typhon while ruling Egypt justly. Typhon cuts his body into six-and-twenty pieces and gives the pieces to his confederates so that they share in the guilt.

l: funeral of Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: After Osiris's death, Isis and Mercury celebrate his funeral with sacrifices and divine honors. Isis later directs the priests to bury his reconstructed body and to honor him as a god.

l: battle between Isis and Typhon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Isis and Orus fight Typhon and his accomplices near a river close to the town called Anthea in Arabia. They defeat Typhon, after which Isis possesses the kingdom of Egypt.

l: Egyptian priests, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: The Egyptian priests initially keep the manner of Osiris's death secret in their registers. Isis assigns them the burial and worship of Osiris, gives them a third of the country for their support, and they preserve his rites and mourn him through the sacred animals.

l: Apis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Apis is one of two sacred bulls consecrated to Osiris. The Egyptians generally regard Apis as a god.

l: Mnevis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Mnevis is the other sacred bull consecrated to Osiris. The Egyptians generally regard Mnevis as a god.

l: sacred bulls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Apis and Mnevis are sacred bulls consecrated to Osiris and worshipped as gods by the Egyptians. Bulls are honored because cattle are described as especially useful in sowing corn and other tillage.

l: Osiris's body, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Typhon cuts Osiris's body into six-and-twenty pieces. Isis finds all the pieces except the privy-members, joins the recovered parts with wax and aromatic spices, and restores them to the shape of a man.

l: Osiris's tomb, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris's tomb is claimed in more than one place. Some Egyptians say he is buried at Memphis, while others identify a revered tomb on the island of the Nile near Philas, also called the Holy Field.

l: Osiris cult mysteries and rites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris is worshipped as a god through sacrifices, mystical ceremonies, priestly mourning, and the veneration of consecrated animals. His privy-member is also represented by an image in temples and adored in rites, a practice the text connects with the Greek name Phallus.

l: agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. 11.
s: Osiris teaches husbandry and tillage in Ethiopia and assigns Triptolemus the cultivation of land in Attica. He is credited with spreading useful food and drink, including a barley drink for places where vines do not grow.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The unit presents Egyptian priests' and Egyptians' accounts of Osiris, Isis, their worship, and the antiquity of Egyptian history, contrasting them with Greek traditions. It claims that Orpheus transferred Egyptian accounts of Osiris and Bacchus into Greece, associating Dionysius with the Greek story of Semele, Cadmus, and Jupiter. It distinguishes an ancient Egyptian Hercules from the later son of Alcmena and attributes to Egypt the origins of several Greek figures, rites, customs, and colonies. It also describes Isis's healing powers, the reigns and chronology of Egyptian gods, and Egyptian claims about colonization, while noting that many of these reports lack sufficient evidence.

l: Osiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Osiris is identified with Bacchus, Dionysius, Serapis, Pluto, Ammon, Jupiter, and Pan. Egyptian priests say that he was not born at Thebes in Boeotia but was an ancient Egyptian god, the husband and brother of Isis, and the father of Orus. His inscriptions describe him as the eldest son of Saturn and as a conqueror and civilizer who traveled through many nations.

l: Isis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Isis is described as the wife and sister of Osiris, the mother of Orus, and a former ruler of Egypt who governed justly after avenging Osiris's death. She is credited with discovering grain, inventing medicines, healing the sick, raising Orus from the dead, and making him immortal. She is identified with Ceres, Thesmophorus, Luna, Juno, and Io, and is said to have been buried at Memphis, although other burial places are reported.

l: Egyptian priests, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Egyptian priests reckon more than ten thousand years, or nearly twenty-three thousand lunar years, from Osiris and Isis or from the earliest divine reigns to Alexander's time. They reject the Greek account that Osiris was born at Thebes in Boeotia and attribute Greek gods, heroes, rites, and colonies to Egypt. They also preserve accounts of divine reigns, Egyptian chronology, and the origins of Egyptian religious customs.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The Egyptians report that their gods and heroes were ancient Egyptians whose identities and customs were later claimed or adapted by the Greeks. They say that Egypt sent colonies throughout the world and that Egyptian customs influenced circumcision, social organization, religious rites, and political traditions. Their reports about foreign origins are presented as claims that the text considers insufficiently supported in many cases.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Egypt is presented as the original home of Osiris, Isis, Hercules, Perseus, and other figures later associated with Greek traditions. It is described as fertile and protected from a worldwide drought, while its upper region is characterized as a wilderness inhabited by wild beasts. Egypt is also portrayed as the source of colonies, religious rites, social divisions, and medical knowledge.

l: Orpheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Orpheus is said to have been initiated in Egypt into the mysteries of Bacchus or Dionysius. Because he was highly esteemed by the Thebans and skilled in music and theology, he allegedly transferred the birth and rites of the Egyptian god into Greece and taught that Dionysius or Osiris was the son of Jupiter and Semele.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Bacchus is identified with Dionysius and Osiris. The text says that Orpheus learned the sacred mysteries of Bacchus in Egypt and transferred his birth and rites into Greek tradition.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Dionysius is identified with Osiris and Bacchus. Greek mysteries are said to have taught that he was begotten by Jupiter through Semele, although the Egyptian account treats this as a later Greek alteration of Osiris's history.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Thebes in Boeotia is described as the place where Greek tradition falsely claimed that Osiris was born. The Thebans are said to have honored Orpheus, whose friendship with them helped lead to the transfer of Osiris's birth and rites into Greece.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Jupiter is presented in the Greek account as the father of Osiris or Dionysius through Semele. He is also named as one of the gods against whom the giants rebelled and with whom Osiris was associated in Egyptian identifications.

l: Semele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, is said in the Greek tradition to have conceived Osiris or Dionysius by Jupiter. The Egyptian-derived account explains this story as a fabrication used to honor Osiris and conceal Semele's shame after she gave birth to a child resembling Osiris.

l: Cadmus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Cadmus is said to have been born at Thebes in Egypt and to have been the father of Semele. After hearing of her unusual child, he allegedly wrapped the infant in gold, established sacrifices to it as a manifestation of Osiris, and spread the story that Jupiter was its father.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The Greeks are accused by the Egyptian priests of appropriating Egyptian gods, demigods, heroes, rites, and customs. Their traditions are said to have transferred Osiris, Isis, Hercules, Perseus, and other figures into Greek settings, while Greek institutions and mysteries are repeatedly compared with Egyptian ones.

l: Osiris cult mysteries and rites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The mysteries and rites of Osiris are said to have been carried from Egypt into Greece by Orpheus. Greek rites declared that Dionysius or Osiris was born from Semele by Jupiter, and the text attributes this development partly to Greek ignorance and partly to the desire to regard the god as Greek.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The Egyptians distinguish an ancient Hercules, said to be the son of Jupiter, from the later Hercules who was the son of Alcmena and was initially called Alceus. The ancient Hercules is credited with fighting giants, freeing the earth from wild beasts, civilizing lands, and setting up a pillar in Africa, while the later Hercules is said to have adopted the name in rivalry with him.

l: the giants of Phlegraea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The giants are described as vast-bodied men who existed in the time of Isis and fought against Jupiter and Osiris. The Egyptians place them near the beginning of mankind and say they were destroyed for their war against the gods, whereas the Greek chronology places Hercules's battle with giants much later.

l: Ceres, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Ceres is identified with Isis and is associated with grain, agriculture, and the Eleusinian rites. The text says that Egyptian rites of Ceres were taught at Eleusis and that Ceres was believed to have come to Attica and given the Athenians grain during a drought.

l: Orus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Orus is described as the son of Osiris and Isis and the last of the gods to reign in Egypt after Osiris's translation. Isis allegedly raised him from the dead after he was killed by the Titans and made him immortal; he is identified with Apollo and credited with benefiting humanity through medicine and divination.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The Athenians are said by the Egyptians to have descended from the Saites of Egypt. Their social division into three orders, religious rites, customs, and some of their leaders are presented as resembling or deriving from Egyptian institutions.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Athens is described as having received Egyptian grain during a severe drought through Erechtheus. The city is also said to have adopted Egyptian rites and mysteries of Ceres and to have been governed according to social divisions resembling those of Egypt.

l: Erechtheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Erechtheus, described as an Egyptian king of Athens, allegedly transported grain from Egypt during a worldwide drought. After the Athenians benefited from this act, he was made king and introduced the festivals, rites, and mysteries of Ceres at Eleusis.

l: Egyptian theology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Egyptian theology identifies several Greek and Egyptian gods with one another, including Isis with Ceres and Osiris with Dionysius, Pluto, Ammon, Jupiter, and Pan. It also includes traditions about divine reigns, sacred inscriptions, the origins of religious rites, and the travels and deeds of Osiris and Hercules.

l: Egyptian colonization, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: The Egyptians claim that colonies from Egypt settled in Babylon, Argos, Colchos, among the Jews, and at Athens. Belus is said to have led a colony to Babylon, Danaus to Argos, and the Athenians to have descended from the Saites; the text concludes that these claims are not supported by sufficient evidence.

l: healing and medicine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Isis is credited with discovering medicines and remedies and with healing people through appearances in dreams. The text says that she cured people considered incurable, restored sight and bodily strength, and taught Orus medicine and divination.

l: Egyptian chronology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, From Osiris and Isis, to the reign of Alexander the Great, who
s: Egyptian priests reckon more than twenty-three thousand years from the reign of Sol to Alexander's passage into Asia, while other calculations give more than ten thousand years or nearly twenty-three thousand lunar years from Osiris and Isis to Alexander. The text explains the extraordinary lengths of divine reigns by suggesting that earlier Egyptians counted lunar or shortened years rather than solar years.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Diodorus Siculus describes Egypt’s natural boundaries, population, cities, and resources. He explains the course of the Nile, its cataracts, islands, channels, mouths, and the formation of the Delta. The unit also discusses Egyptian plants, animals such as the crocodile and river horse, and the Nile’s annual inundation. It presents the inundation as the basis of Egypt’s fertile soil, abundant agriculture, and prosperity.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Egypt is described as lying mostly toward the south and as being naturally fortified by deserts, mountains, cataracts, marshes, the Lake Serbon, and the sea. It is portrayed as a long country with a densely populated and highly productive land, formerly containing more than eighteen thousand cities.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Nile flows from the south toward the north from unknown springs near the borders of Ethiopia. It makes many turns, islands, channels, and mouths, and is described as the greatest and most beneficial of rivers, bringing fertile soil and water to Egypt.

l: Lake Serbon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Lake Serbon lies between Coelo-Syria and Egypt and is narrow, extremely deep, and about two hundred furlongs long. Sand blown by southern winds makes its surface resemble dry land, causing people and even whole armies to sink into its mud and water.

l: Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Ethiopia contains the remote regions and mountains from which the Nile descends, though its extreme heat and deserts make the river’s springs inaccessible. It is also associated with the region around Meroe island and with mines, ebony trees, and precious stones.

l: Meroe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Meroe island is a large island formed by the Nile near Ethiopia, with a city of the same name. It is described as being shield-shaped, containing many cities, and possessing mines of gold, silver, iron, and brass, as well as ebony trees and precious stones.

l: Delta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Delta is formed where the Nile divides into several channels in Egypt and is named for its resemblance to the Greek letter. Its seven mouths empty into the ocean, and its dikes, sluices, fertile soil, and abundant crops make it the sweetest and most pleasant part of Egypt.

l: cataracts of the Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The cataracts are steep, rocky passages where the Nile plunges violently through narrow gulfs. Their whirlpools and rapids make navigation dangerous and prevent ships from sailing upstream, with the greatest cataract lying on the borders of Ethiopia and Egypt.

l: overflowing of the Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The Nile inundation begins at the summer solstice, rises until the autumn equinox, and gradually falls again toward the winter solstice. It spreads water and new soil over Egypt, enabling farmers to irrigate fields easily and producing abundant crops with little labor.

l: crocodile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The crocodile is described as growing from a small egg to a creature up to sixteen cubits long, with a heavily scaled body, powerful teeth, and destructive claws. It devours people and animals near the river, but its eggs are broken by the ichneumon; some Egyptians also worship it as a god.

l: river horse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: The river horse is described as a large, four-footed, cloven-hoofed animal that lives both on land and in water. It feeds on grass and corn at night and is hunted by groups who wound it with iron instruments and let it bleed to death.

l: Egyptian soil, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Egyptian soil is continually renewed by the mud carried in the Nile’s yearly overflow. The deposited soil makes low and hollow grounds into rich marshes and supports abundant roots, fruits, herbs, grain, vines, and pasture.

l: Egyptian agriculture, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. III.
s: Egyptian agriculture depends heavily on the Nile’s gentle flooding and on dikes, sluices, and irrigation devices. Farmers can sow or lightly plow after the waters recede, obtain large crops with little labor, grow vines and other fruits, and pasture animals on the watered land.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: The unit examines the Nile, its headwaters, course, and annual overflowing, reviewing and criticizing explanations offered by ancient writers. Herodotus, Ephorus, Anaxagoras, Democritus, the philosophers of Memphis, and Agartharchides of Cnidus are among those whose theories are discussed. The account rejects explanations based on the Etesian winds, Ethiopian snow, Egypt’s underground waters, and an opposite inhabited zone. Agartharchides’ explanation, that continual summer rains fall in the mountainous parts of Ethiopia, is presented as coming nearest to the truth.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: The Nile is described as the greatest river in the world, with distinctive properties, an uncertain source, and a course that eventually empties into the sea. It rises in summer, overflows Egypt, and is said to be at full height before reaching Egypt after flowing through Ethiopia for more than six thousand furlongs.

l: overflowing of the Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: The Nile begins to swell around the summer solstice and falls again after the autumnal equinox. The unit reviews several explanations for this annual overflowing and concludes that the abundance of summer rains in the mountainous parts of Ethiopia comes nearest to explaining it.

l: causes of the Nile's flooding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Proposed causes include obstruction by the Etesian winds, melting Ethiopian snow, the sun’s action, vapors and storms driven toward Ethiopian mountains, waters stored beneath Egypt, rains in an opposite zone, and seasonal underground waters. Most of these explanations are rejected as inconsistent with observation or reasoning.

l: Nile headwaters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: No writer is said to have seen the Nile’s headwaters or to have heard a reliable report from anyone who had seen them. The Troglodites say that the Nile is formed from streams issuing from many springs, while the inhabitants of Meroe call it Astapus, signifying water issuing from a place of darkness.

l: Herodotus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Herodotus is praised as industrious and knowledgeable in general history, but his explanations of the Nile are called doubtful and sometimes contradictory. He says that the Nile rises from a lake, runs through Ethiopia, and decreases in winter because the sun then passes over Africa and draws water from it.

l: Ephorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Ephorus says that Egypt is raised from the river and contains loose, spongy soil with cavities holding water, which issues out in summer and raises the Nile. His explanation is rejected because the Nile is already high before reaching Egypt and because such cavities could not contain enough water to cause the inundation.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Egypt is described as flat and low, and the Nile’s overflowing covers much of its land. The unit rejects the claim that waters stored in Egypt’s soil cause the flooding, noting that the river passes through rocky and mountainous places before entering Egypt.

l: Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Ethiopia is presented as the region through which the Nile flows before reaching Egypt. Its mountainous parts are said by Agartharchides of Cnidus to receive continual yearly rains from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox.

l: Etesian winds, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Thales attributes the Nile’s flooding to the Etesian winds blocking its mouth and preventing it from flowing into the sea. Democritus also uses the winds in his explanation, but this is rejected because the Nile begins swelling before the winds occur and falls after they have ended.

l: Anaxagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Anaxagoras attributes the Nile’s flooding to melting snow in Ethiopia, an explanation followed by Euripides. The unit rejects this because Ethiopia shows no frost, cold, or other signs of winter when the Nile overflows.

l: Democritus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Democritus says that snow belongs to northern rather than southern regions and that vapors driven by the Etesian winds produce rain on the highest Ethiopian mountains. His explanation is criticized because the Nile swells before the Etesian winds begin and falls after they have passed.

l: Memphis philosophers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: The philosophers in Memphis argue that the Nile receives winter rains from the opposite zone, where it is then winter, and that its water is sweetened by passing through the torrid zone. Their theory is rejected as physically impossible and because boiled water would not support fish or other living creatures.

l: Agartharchides of Cnidus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Agartharchides of Cnidus comes nearest to the true explanation of the Nile’s flooding. He says that continual rains fall in the mountainous parts of Ethiopia from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox, filling the river and causing it to overflow.

l: snow, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Snow is proposed by Anaxagoras and Euripides as the source of the Nile’s summer increase. This explanation is rejected because no frost, cold, or other effects of winter are observed in Ethiopia during the Nile’s overflowing.

l: rainfall in Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, There are great controversies concerning the reasons of the over-
s: Rainfall in the mountainous parts of Ethiopia is presented as the explanation that comes nearest to accounting for the Nile’s summer flooding. Agartharchides says that the rains continue yearly from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Diodorus Siculus describes Egyptian accounts of their earliest food, dwellings, religion, rulers, and royal monuments. The Egyptians are said to have progressed from roots, herbs, fish, and cattle to cultivated fruits and bread, while their kings were credited with discovering necessities of life. The account names Menis as the first human king, describes the building and splendor of Thebes under Busiris's successor, and gives an extensive description of Osymandyas's sepulchre. It also records the destruction and removal of Egyptian treasures by Cambyses and the Persians.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Diodorus Siculus reports what the Egyptian priests and other writers say about Egypt's ancient customs, rulers, temples, and sepulchres. He states that he himself came into Egypt during the reign of Ptolemy, who took the name of Dionysius the younger, and later during the reign of Ptolemy Lagus.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: The Egyptians are said to have first lived on roots, herbs, and colewort leaves, especially agrostis, and later to have eaten fish, cattle, cultivated fruits, and bread made from lotus. They made early dwellings from reeds and worshipped the gods with agrostis in memory of its usefulness.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Egypt is described through accounts of its ancient rulers, cities, temples, sepulchres, and forms of worship. Most of its kings were natives, though some rulers were Ethiopians, Persians, or Macedonians.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: The Nile is mentioned as supplying the Egyptians with fish, especially after its inundation had receded within its former bounds. The account also refers to the river in describing a fortified place represented in the sculptures of Osymandyas's sepulchre.

l: the gods and demi-gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: The gods and demi-gods are said to have ruled Egypt for almost eighteen thousand years, with Orys, the son of Isis, as the last of them. Gods are also credited in Egyptian accounts with building cities in Egypt and naming them after themselves.

l: Egyptian kings, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Egyptian kings were credited with discovering things necessary for human support, and kingship was said originally to have been given to those most useful and serviceable to the people rather than inherited. Menis was identified as the first king after the gods, while later kings were recorded for their buildings, conquests, worship, and monuments.

l: Menis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Menis was said to be the first human king of Egypt after the gods. He taught the people to worship the gods and introduced richer coverings for beds and tables, as well as a delicate and sumptuous way of living; his reputation was later clouded by Gnephachthus's curse on luxury.

l: Busiris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Busiris was followed by eight descendants, the last of whom, bearing the same name, built the great city that the Egyptians called Heliopolis and the Greeks called Thebes.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Thebes is described as a city about one hundred and forty furlongs in circuit, filled with public buildings, magnificent temples, rich donations, and private houses several stories high. It was famed for its wealth and grandeur, its temples and monuments, and its supposed hundred gates and twenty thousand war chariots.

l: Osymandyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Osymandyas was associated with one of the greatest ancient royal sepulchres. Sculptures there represented his wars against the revolting Bactrians, his sacrifices and triumphs, his offerings to the gods, and the administration of justice.

l: Osymandyas's sepulchre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Osymandyas's sepulchre was described as ten furlongs in circuit, with large marble porticoes, galleries supported by colossal stone figures, statues, sculptures, an altar, a court of judgment, a library called the cure of the Mind, rooms containing food and sacred animals, and a royal burial chamber. Its summit had a gold border measuring three hundred and sixty-five cubits, marked with the days of the year and astronomical observations.

l: Cambyses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Cambyses and the Persians are said to have burned the temples of Egypt and carried away their silver, gold, ivory, and precious stones. Cambyses also carried away the gold border from the top of Osymandyas's monument.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: The Persians ruled Egypt for one hundred and thirty-five years, counting periods of Egyptian revolt caused by harsh governors and impiety toward the Egyptian gods. They removed Egyptian treasures and brought them to Asia, where they used Egyptian workmen in the construction of palaces at Persepolis, Susa, and elsewhere in Media.

l: Egyptian royal succession, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Egyptian priests were said to preserve temple registers listing the kings successively across many generations, including their greatness, dispositions, and actions. The account gives totals of Egyptian, Ethiopian, Persian, and Macedonian rulers and continues the succession down to Amasis.

l: Egyptian religion and worship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Egyptian religion and worship included offerings to the gods, temple building, reverence for sacred animals, and the use of agrostis in sacrifices. Menis was credited with teaching divine worship, while the sepulchre of Osymandyas displayed offerings to the gods and proclaimed the king's piety and justice.

l: Egyptian royal monuments, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. / BOOK I.
s: Egyptian royal monuments included temples, sepulchres, obelisks, colossal statues, and richly decorated public buildings. The monuments of Thebes were described as exceptionally ancient, costly, and magnificent, although many treasures were later taken by Cambyses and the Persians.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Thebans claim to be the world’s most ancient philosophers and astrologers, and they describe their methods for measuring time and predicting eclipses. Uchoreus, the eighth king of his line, founded Memphis near the Nile’s division into the Delta and fortified it with ramparts and trenches. Memphis later became the preferred royal residence, while Thebes declined in magnificence. Meris built a vast lake and irrigation system near Memphis, using it to regulate the Nile’s waters and benefit Egypt’s agriculture.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Thebans boast that they were the most ancient philosophers and astrologers in the world and the first to establish exact rules for philosophy and astrology. They claim that their location helped them observe the rising and setting of the stars, calculate time by the sun, and accurately predict solar and lunar eclipses.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: Thebes was initially the royal center, but its magnificence began to decline after later kings preferred Memphis and moved the court there. The Thebans regarded their country as a center of ancient learning and astronomical observation.

l: philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Thebans claim to have been the first people to discover exact rules for improving philosophy.

l: astrology, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Thebans claim to have founded the exact rules of astrology. They observed the stars and eclipses and used their observations to make prognostications about future events.

l: Uchoreus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: Uchoreus was the eighth king of his line and built Memphis. He selected its location near the Nile’s branches and fortified it with a great earthen rampart and a deep trench.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: Memphis was founded by Uchoreus near the head of the Nile’s branches, where the river forms the Delta. Its rampart and surrounding trench protected it from the river’s inundations and from enemies, and many later kings preferred it to Thebes as their royal residence.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Nile divided into several branches near Memphis and formed the region called Delta. It flowed around the city, flooded its southern side, and was later managed through trenches, sluices, and the lake built by Meris to regulate irrigation.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: Egypt was said in a fable to have received its name from Egyptus, who was born from the union of the Nile, in the form of a bull, and the founder’s daughter. Meris later ruled Egypt and constructed a major lake and waterworks for its benefit.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The Egyptians are described as caring little for the brief duration of earthly life and valuing the reputation of virtuous conduct after death. They called houses for the living inns and tombs everlasting habitations, and therefore devoted more care to sepulchres than to houses.

l: Meris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: Meris became king of Egypt after twelve generations and built a magnificent portico at Memphis. He also dug a vast lake and a connecting trench so that excess Nile water could be stored and later directed into the fields through sluices.

l: lake of Myris or Meris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Thebans boast they were the most antient philosophers and
s: The lake of Myris or Meris was built near Memphis to receive excess water from the Nile and help prevent both destructive flooding and inadequate irrigation. It was described as three thousand six hundred furlongs in circumference, with a connecting trench eighty furlongs long, and its fish provided a daily talent of silver for the king’s wife’s clothing.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: The unit concerns Sesostris, who was trained with boys born on the same day and later became king of Egypt. He organized a large Egyptian army, conquered territories in Africa, Asia, and Europe, and sought to subdue the whole world before ending his expedition in Thrace. After returning to Egypt, he built temples, canals, dykes, fortifications, obelisks, statues, and other public works, while rewarding his soldiers and imposing tributes on conquered nations. He later became blind and voluntarily ended his life after reigning for thirty-three years.

l: Sesostris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Sesostris was trained from childhood for command and later became king of Egypt. He conquered many territories, organized a vast empire, built extensive public works, and was celebrated for his military achievements and generosity. After reigning for thirty-three years, he became blind and voluntarily ended his life.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: The Egyptians were organized under Sesostris into thirty-six provinces, each governed by an appointed official. They supplied the army, benefited from the conquest and public works, and were generally spared labor on Sesostris's temple projects, which were performed by captives.

l: Sesostris's childhood companions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Sesostris's childhood companions were born on the same day as he was and were raised with him under the same education, discipline, and exercises. They became his commanders and fellow soldiers, numbering more than seventeen hundred, and received large estates in the richest parts of Egypt in return for attending him in war.

l: Egyptian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: The Egyptian army numbered six hundred thousand infantry, twenty-four thousand cavalry, and twenty-seven thousand war chariots. It conquered Ethiopia and much of Asia and returned after the nine-year expedition loaded with riches, captives, and spoils.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Egypt was divided into thirty-six provinces and was strengthened by Sesostris's administration, conquests, canals, embankments, and fortifications. The country gained wealth, trade, provisions, peace, and security from his expedition and works.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Asia was invaded and largely conquered by Sesostris. His forces passed the Ganges, traversed India to the ocean, subdued the Scythians as far as the Tanais, and brought the remaining parts of Asia and many islands of the Cyclades under his rule.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Memphis was connected to the canal works extending toward the sea. Sesostris placed statues of himself and his wife, along with statues of his sons, in the temple of Vulcan at Memphis.

l: Alexander's conquest of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: The Egyptian expedition lasted nine years and extended from Ethiopia and the Red Sea to Asia, the Scythians, the Cyclades, and parts of Europe. Sesostris required conquered nations to send annual presents and tributes to Egypt and returned with captives and extensive spoils.

l: Sesostris's attempted world conquest, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: After earlier victories in Arabia and Libya, Sesostris planned to conquer the whole world. He advanced through Africa, Asia, and Europe but stopped his expedition in Thrace after facing difficult passages and shortages of provisions.

l: construction of Egyptian public works, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: After his conquests, Sesostris constructed temples, embankments, canals, fortifications, a large cedar ship, obelisks, and statues. These works were intended both to preserve his fame and to provide Egypt with practical benefits and security.

l: temples of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Sesostris built a temple in every Egyptian city to the god most worshipped there and adorned the temples with rich presents and enemy spoils. Captives performed the labor, and inscriptions stated that no natives had been forced to work there.

l: Egyptian canals and dykes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Sesostris raised banks and mounds and moved low-lying cities onto them to protect people and animals from the inundation. He also cut deep dykes from the river between Memphis and the sea to facilitate the movement of grain, provisions, and merchandise, while the canals made Egypt harder to invade.

l: Egyptian imperial power and glory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Seven descents after, (they say), Sesostris reigned, who excelled
s: Sesostris's imperial power was displayed through his conquests, tributary system, monumental works, and the submission of foreign kings and princes. His fame remained strong after his death, and a priest later argued that Darius had not surpassed his achievements.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Sesostris the Second succeeded his father but accomplished nothing notable in war and became blind, supposedly because of impiety toward the Nile; after ten years he was cured through an oracle's instructions and erected two obelisks. Actisanes, king of Ethiopia, conquered the tyrannical Ammosis and ruled Egypt moderately, while later Egyptian kings included Mendes, Proteus, Remphis, Chemmis, Cephres, Mycerinus, Bocchoris, and Sabacos. Chemmis built the Great Pyramid, Cephres built the second pyramid, and Mycerinus began the third pyramid. After Sabacos abandoned the throne, twelve Egyptian nobles ruled jointly until Psammetichus defeated the others with foreign troops; more than two hundred thousand Egyptian soldiers then migrated to Ethiopia after being dishonored.

l: Sesostris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Sesostris the Second succeeded his father and took the same name, but did nothing remarkable by his arms. He became blind, was eventually cured after following an oracle's instructions, married a gardener's wife, punished adulteresses, and erected two large obelisks at the command of the oracle.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Egypt passed through successive rulers, including Ethiopian domination under Actisanes and later native kings. After Sabacos returned to Ethiopia, twelve nobles jointly ruled Egypt, until Psammetichus gained the whole kingdom.

l: Actisanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Actisanes, king of Ethiopia, invaded Ammosis and conquered him after most of Ammosis's oppressed subjects revolted. He ruled Egypt moderately, punished robbers by cutting off their noses and banishing them to Rhinocorura, and built that city for them.

l: Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Ethiopia ruled Egypt after Actisanes conquered Ammosis. More than two hundred thousand Egyptian soldiers later migrated to Ethiopia, where they settled in a rich and fruitful land and divided it among themselves.

l: the Egyptian labyrinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Mendes built a sepulchre called a labyrinth, which was difficult to leave without a skilled guide. The text says that Daedalus admired it and made a similar labyrinth for Minos in Crete, while the Egyptian labyrinth remained intact.

l: Nile, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Sesostris the Second was said to have incurred blindness by throwing a javelin at the Nile. During the reign of the later king Nile, canals and dykes made the river more useful, and it received the name Nile after him, having previously been called Egyptus.

l: Chemmis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Chemmis, the eighth king after Remphis, was from Memphis and reigned fifty years. He built the greatest of the three pyramids.

l: the pyramids of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The pyramids stood toward Libya, one hundred and twenty furlongs from Memphis and forty-five from the Nile, and were counted among the seven wonders of the world. The text emphasizes their enormous size, costly labor, durable construction, and disputed origins, while saying that the three last kings built additional pyramids for their wives.

l: the Great Pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Great Pyramid was attributed to Chemmis and had a square base measuring seven hundred feet on each side and a height of more than six hundred feet. It was built of solid marble, reportedly with three hundred and sixty thousand workers over nearly twenty years, and its laborers' herbs and onions were said to have cost more than sixteen hundred talents.

l: the second pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The second pyramid was built by Cephres, or according to some by his son Chabryis, in imitation of the first. It resembled the Great Pyramid in structure and workmanship but was considerably smaller, with each side of its base measuring one furlong.

l: Mycerinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Mycerinus, also called Cherinus, succeeded the builder of the Great Pyramid and began a third pyramid, but died before it was completed. The text portrays him as a gentle ruler who sought his subjects' love, honored the gods, and aided people whom he judged to have been wronged in court.

l: the third pyramid, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The third pyramid was begun by Mycerinus and had a base measuring three hundred feet on each side. Its lower fifteen stories were of black marble like that of Thebes, while the remainder used the same stone as the other pyramids; it was unfinished when Mycerinus died.

l: Amasis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Amasis is mentioned as a king who reigned many years after Psammetichus and transplanted Psammetichus's mercenary soldiers from their settlement near Pelusium to Memphis.

l: Sabacos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Sabacos, an Ethiopian king, exceeded his predecessors in worship of the gods and kindness to his subjects. He replaced death sentences with forced labor, then abdicated and returned to Ethiopia after refusing to kill the priests as directed by repeated dreams.

l: the twelve kings of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: After Sabacos's departure and a two-year anarchy, twelve chief nobles of Egypt swore an oath, made laws, and jointly assumed royal power. They ruled amicably for fifteen years and began a grand common sepulchre, but all except Psammetichus later lost their sovereignty.

l: Psammetichus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Psammetichus, one of the twelve kings and ruler of a coastal province, grew wealthy through trade with Phoenicians and Greeks. He defeated the other kings near Moniemphis with hired soldiers from Arabia, Caria, and Ionia, gained all Egypt, encouraged foreign trade, allied with Athens and other Greeks, and had his son taught Greek learning.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Greeks traded with Psammetichus's coastal province and were among the foreigners whom he welcomed into Egypt. Psammetichus allied with Athens and other Greeks and had his son instructed in Greek learning.

l: Psammetichus's mercenary army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Psammetichus hired soldiers from Arabia, Caria, and Ionia, and used them to defeat the other kings near Moniemphis. He rewarded these mercenaries generously, settled them at Stratopedon near the mouth of Pelusium, and relied on them in governing Egypt.

l: the Egyptian soldiers who migrated to Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: More than two hundred thousand Egyptian soldiers revolted after Psammetichus placed foreign troops in the army's right wing and the Egyptians in the left. They rejected the king's attempts to recall them, marched into Ethiopia, and settled there after declaring that their arms and fertility would provide them with a new country and families.

l: the Egyptian revolt and migration to Ethiopia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The revolt began when Psammetichus dishonored the native Egyptian soldiers by assigning them the less favored position in an army serving in Syria. The migrants resisted the king's appeals, entered Ethiopia, and divided a rich and fruitful territory among themselves.

l: Memphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Memphis was the site of a senate called by the twelve nobles after Sabacos's departure. Psammetichus later built a portico and wall at the temple there, and Amasis eventually moved Psammetichus's mercenary soldiers to Memphis.

l: foreign trade in Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Psammetichus was the first Egyptian king described as encouraging foreigners to trade in Egypt. His commerce with Phoenicians and Greeks enriched his province, increased his influence abroad, and led him to provide safe conduct for foreign visitors.

l: Cambyses' conquest of Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Cambyses' conquest of Egypt is mentioned in the chapter heading as the event marking the end of Amasis's reign. The provided passage does not narrate the conquest itself.
